title: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
description: Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from fi
body: Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:People who earned at least £50,271 for three of five years immediately before applying for settlementCare workers who earned at least £25,000 a year while meeting their visa conditions and arrived in the UK before May 2025"Skilled" public service workers in health and education, such as doctors, nurses, teachers and social workersOther health and education public service workers who fall below this skill level, for example nursing auxiliaries and teaching assistants, if they arrived in the UK before May 2025People from Hong Kong who hold British National (Overseas) statusPeople earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.Adults with a criminal record will be refused settlement, with discretion to refuse cases where the offence was committed when the applicant was under 18.To qualify for settlement, migrants will generally also have to meet other conditions, including:Speak English to a high standardOwe no debt to the government, such as unpaid taxesEarn at least £12,571 a year for at least three years, aligned with the threshold for paying income taxA partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income  requirement.The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

schema.headline: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?

title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
description: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabiliti
body: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure."There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible."I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility."The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace."Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said."Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security."Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.  Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

schema.headline: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

title: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
description: Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga.Regulator the Financial Conduct Au
body: Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga.Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme.That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year.But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit.The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case.Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice."Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means."Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced.With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost. Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait"."By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson."Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them."The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks".But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer.The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers, external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders.It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed.The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes:Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smallerClaimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid moreAccepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsmanThe Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty."But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered."These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said.The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February.Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed". Three lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance - are also challenging the scheme.The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled from 16 February to 3 March.Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained can still complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free, external.

schema.headline: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends

title: Indian tourist killed after helicopters collide near Everest base camp
description: An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed t
body: An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man  killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said. It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.

schema.headline: Indian tourist killed after helicopters collide near Everest base camp

title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
description: The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, ana
body: The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found.Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report.The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic."This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation.Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic. Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more.So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage".Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting.The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults.Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sunk to one-in-four, the lowest level on record.In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%."Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added.This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found. Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade".Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs". "But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added.

schema.headline: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why

title: Florida plane crash investigators say jet may have broken apart before impact as family named
description: Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.The Learj
body: Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida and killed all nine onboard may have broken off while it was in the air.The Learjet 60 had been bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old co-pilot, were among those who died on Sunday.The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on the road in Palm Beach.The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time (17:50 GMT)."The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, had become partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area."We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was onboard at the time of the crash and whether it can be recovered.Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before it crashed.In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and nanny Anita Maria Cetina. The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the crash.Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."Filgueiras had spoken of her pride at receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school in an interview with a local affiliate of CBS News in 2023."I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes but I can't drive a car - I mean, I can, but a lot of people think it's funny."A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."He was married with two children, US media report.

schema.headline: Florida plane crash investigators say jet may have broken apart before impact as family named

title: Hampshire Reform UK councillor charged with rape and sexual assault
description: The leader of Reform UK in Hampshire has been charged with 35 offences against four victims over a 13 year period, including 12 counts of rape.The Cro
body: The leader of Reform UK in Hampshire has been charged with 35 offences against four victims over a 13 year period, including 12 counts of rape.The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said it had charged George Madgwick with the offences, which it said took place between 2008 and 2021 in Portsmouth and Wales.It said the 37-year-old faced charges including rape, sexual assault, controlling or coercive behaviour, and making indecent images of a child against four victims - who were aged 16 and 17 at the time.Reform UK said Madgwick had been suspended "with immediate effect". He is due to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 25 November.Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said its investigation into Madgwick began on 24 July 2025, after receiving a report of a sexual offence.The force said it first arrested him on 6 January 2026, before he was charged by the CPS on Tuesday.In total, Madgwick, who is from the the Anchorage Park area of Portsmouth, has been charged with 12 counts of rape, two counts of assault by penetration and two of sexual assault.Madgwick has also been charged with two counts of making indecent images of children, two of controlling or coercive behaviour and eight of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.He faces one charge each of causing or inciting sexual exploitation of a child, distributing an indecent image of a child, stalking, making threats to kill, false imprisonment, theft and criminal damage.A spokesperson for the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court."We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in any way prejudice these proceedings."The 37-year-old councillor represents North East Havant on Hampshire County Council and Paulsgrove on Portsmouth City Council.Last month, he was featured in the the ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform - after which he accused the broadcaster of  "electoral interference".In the programme, he was featured voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group.He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections.

schema.headline: Hampshire Reform UK councillor charged with rape and sexual assault

title: The zeptoverse: what is it and how will it transform physics?
description: Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.Scientists know it is there because its gravitational
body: Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions. One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter."We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News. He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles."And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts."I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget. UK research hit by cuts despite record science fundingProf Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important". But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project."It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said. The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage. "However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

schema.headline: The zeptoverse: what is it and how will it transform physics?

title: Jesus de Miguel: Tenerife striker dies after on-field collision
description: Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.The forward suffered
body: Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge. De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.Reuters reported on Tuesday that police in Spain have opened an investigation for possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death. Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry."Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true" Tenerife said. "There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel. The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account. Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, said: "With broken hearts and devastated, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his team-mates, friends, and to CD Tenerife."Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way."We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss."My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."

schema.headline: Jesus de Miguel: Tenerife striker dies after on-field collision

title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
description: Figure caption, 'I've always looked in bins for clothes'ByChris MarshallBusiness reporterUpdated 7 hours agoDarryl Baker was shocked to see piles of c
body: Figure caption, 'I've always looked in bins for clothes'ByChris MarshallBusiness reporterUpdated 7 hours agoDarryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."Image source, Darryl BakerImage caption, Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sellIn addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket.Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three.'I'm a bit of a Robin Hood'Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years."I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever."Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds."Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says.Image source, Phil HarveyImage caption, Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other itemsJeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay.Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year".'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it'While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online.Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells.Image source, Millie DiamondImage caption, Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfitsShe estimates that one dress she found was worth £600."I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it."Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes."'I haven't bought shampoo for years'For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them.This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money."Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items. Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says.Image source, Charlotte BayfordImage caption, Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charityBut is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law?Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita."Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges.In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land, external.In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances. "In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says. "But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin. If in doubt, the safest approach is to ask the owner or business for permission."

schema.headline: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving

title: When will we know who won the US midterms?
description: ByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporter  and Deirdre FinnertyMillions of Americans are voting in midterm elections that could reshape the balance of
body: ByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporter  and Deirdre FinnertyMillions of Americans are voting in midterm elections that could reshape the balance of power in Washington. The outcome determines which party - US President Donald Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress. Once polls close, it is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks. Here's what you need to know.When will we know the results and who controls Congress?Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate. To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.First results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT). They won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump. There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed. This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections. The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.When did we know the results in 2022?In 2022, Republicans and Democrats were still in a tight race for control of the US Congress on 9 November, a day after the midterms. While Republicans were favourites to win the House of Representatives, the fight for the Senate remained on a knife-edge.The full picture took several days. CBS News projected Republicans had secured the 218 seats needed for a majority in the House on 17 November.Counting in a crucial Senate race in Nevada took four days. The Democrats' narrow victory in the state brought them to 50 seats, allowing them to retain control of the Senate because then Vice-President Kamala Harris held a tie-breaking vote.Georgia's Senate contest had to be settled by a run-off election because no candidate passed the 50% mark in November. The results were not available until 7 December, when Democrats won this seat.What are the key races to watch in 2026?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ashley Hinson, who was once a local news reporter, is up against ex-basketballer Josh Turek in Iowa in a key raceIf Democrats fail to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, winning a majority in the Senate becomes much harder. Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, is up against Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent. (Michigan was initially classified as a "toss-up" by Cook Political Report, but was reclassified as "leans Democrat" the day before the vote).But polls have suggested Democrats have a chance even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.The current Republican majority in the House, the lower chamber, is thin. They have 218 representatives, plus one independent who votes with them.Some of the most closely-watched races in the House are in east-coast states, according to the Cook Political Report. These include New York's 17th District, Pennsylvania's 8th District and Virginia's 1st District.When do polls close?Image source, Getty ImagesThe results of a voter poll will be released at 17:00 EST (22:00 GMT), which will give us an indication of the issues at the forefront of voters' minds.Then, at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), the first polls close in Kentucky and Indiana. After that, all eyes will be focused on the key battleground states:19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) - Polls close in Ohio, where Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck-and-neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown. Results from this state could give us a clue as to how the night might unfold20:00 EST (01:00 GMT) - Voting ends in the tight Senate race in Maine between Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson and in most of Kansas and Texas21:00 EST (02:00 GMT) - Polls close in Iowa, as well as in Kansas and Texas. In the hours that follow, a picture might start to emerge of whether things are going to plan for the Republicans - or the Democrats01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) - Voting ends in Alaska, the last battleground state. A close Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been making headlines over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballotHow does the vote-counting work?Each state administers its own elections and has its own rules for counting and processing votes.Some states, like Florida, process early and mail ballots prior to election day, while others only begin tabulating on 3 November.Local election officials verify, process and count individual votes, in a process known as canvassing.Most states require a post-election audit that involves a manual count of ballots checked against machine totals, although rules vary across the country. Full hand counts are generally reserved for recounts.Every state and locality has rules which specify who can participate in the canvass, the order in which votes are processed and which parts are open to the public, including how partisan observers can watch the count and, in some states, raise formal challenges.Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesWhat might cause a delay?Tight races will take longer, and create the possibility of recounts being triggered and legal challenges. Mail-in ballots take longer to count, as officials need to process envelopes and verify signatures. More than 30 states allow ballots to be processed before election day, but other states do not. In California, all ballots must be posted before or on election day and will still be counted if they arrive within seven days of the election.In Alaska, ranked-choice voting could mean that tabulations take considerably longer than elsewhere in the country and the controversy over ballots could mean that legal challenges can complicate things.Figure caption, When will we know the US midterm election results?What happens if results are challenged?Once every vote has been included in the final results, and after processes such as recounts have been completed, the election results are certified - first at the local, county, level and then state-wide.The governor then typically signs the certifications for House and Senate winners to be sent to Congress.Results can be challenged. Recounts can be requested by candidates in close races, and in some states recounts are automatically triggered if they fall within a certain margin. Candidates can also file legal election contests alleging irregularities.Congress has the final word. Losing candidates in both House and Senate races can file contests, with slightly different processes in each of the two chambers. Both chambers can, theoretically, refuse to seat someone or order an investigation.When do winners take office?

schema.headline: When will we know who won the US midterms?

title: Boy, 16, arrested over Halloween stabbings in Chandler's Ford
description: Third teen arrested after Halloween party stabbingsImage caption, Police said an unknown group had gained entry to the party on SaturdayByDave Gilyeat
body: Third teen arrested after Halloween party stabbingsImage caption, Police said an unknown group had gained entry to the party on SaturdayByDave GilyeatSouth of EnglandUpdated 59 minutes agoA third teenage boy has been arrested after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.Police said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.One 17-year-old boy remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.A 16-year-old from Bristol has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. He remains in custody, as do two boys arrested on Monday.Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'."And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.Image caption, Police cordons remain in place in Chandler's FordHampshire Police said officers were continuing to review video footage and information provided by witnesses to piece together the movements of those involved on the night.Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie, senior investigating officer, said: "I want to thank everyone who has already come forward to speak about what they saw on the night, or share with us any footage they have."Our team are working incredibly hard to understand what happened and identify anyone who may have been involved."We now have arrested three boys, but we still want to hear from you if you have any information which could assist us. However small it may seem to you, it may be key to our enquiries."'Extremely distressing'The force said throughout the coming week, local officers from the Neighbourhood Policing Team are visiting local schools and colleges to offer further advice and reassurance, as well as to support those directly and indirectly affected by this incident.Ch Insp Rachel Noble, district commander for Eastleigh, said: "The violence witnessed on Saturday night will have undoubtedly been extremely distressing and concerning for everyone who was at the party."It is really important to us that everyone knows what support is available for them, should they want to talk about, and how they can report anything to us so the investigation team can continue with their enquiries."Local officers will also continue to be out in the area of Park Road, so if you do have any concerns or need to speak about anything then do not hesitate to do so when you see them."Get in touchYour Voice

title: Staffordshire's Alton Towers closes World of David Walliams
description: The World of David Walliams attraction at Alton Towers has permanently closed, the theme park has announced.The park's creative team worked with Walli
body: The World of David Walliams attraction at Alton Towers has permanently closed, the theme park has announced.The park's creative team worked with Walliams and HarperCollins Children's Books over a number of years to develop the section of the resort, which opened in 2021."As we are no longer in the main season, guests are encouraged to check the Alton Towers Resort website and app for the latest attraction opening information ahead of their visit," the park said in a statement on its website.Alton Towers says the closure comes as it regularly looks at "elements of our attraction offering".It is understood the decision was made taking into account a range of operational and guest experience considerations.Plans for future use of the area will be announced once they have been confirmed.Among the rides in the Walliams-themed area of the park were Gangsta Granny: The Ride, a 360° special effects attraction, as well as Raj's Bouncy Bottom Burp, Royal Carousel and Flavio's Fabulous Fandango.

title: William Saliba's return gives Mikel Arteta selection headache at Arsenal
description: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta will soon have a big defensive dilemma.But it is one that will be both welcome to the Arsenal boss and the envy of other top
body: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta will soon have a big defensive dilemma.But it is one that will be both welcome to the Arsenal boss and the envy of other top teams across the continent.That's because William Saliba - a key figure in the Gunners' title win last season - is back in training, having missed the entire campaign so far because of a back injury following his early withdrawal in France's World Cup semi-final loss to Spain.The 25-year-old has been one of the Premier League's top defenders in recent seasons but - in his absence - summer signing Ezri Konsa has stepped in seamlessly to help Arsenal back to the top of the table.Indeed, since Konsa's arrival from Aston Villa for £55m, he and Gabriel Magalhaes  have struck up a formidable partnership, with Arsenal again boasting the league's tightest defence, conceding just five goals in nine games.Saliba had been managing his back issue throughout last season but was sent to see a specialist after the World Cup. It was decided he did not need to undergo surgery but would require a lengthy rehabilitation. No timescale on his return was set. The France international had been doing individual training at Arsenal's base but has now returned to full training before their Champions League meeting with Slavia Prague and then, a busy festive schedule looming. Saliba and regular partner Gabriel were a huge reason why the Gunners won the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years last season.Their partnership was the bedrock of Arteta's team, which conceded only 27 league goals. Saliba was then named in the PFA team of the year for the fourth consecutive time. Arsenal have always said that they will be cautious with Saliba's return but his return to fitness will leave Arteta with some tough choices to make in his backline. Such was Arsenal's strength in defence, there were questions about whether they needed to sign Konsa when the Gunners decided to spend £55m on the England international.But the centre-back has been one of the club's best players this season as they sit top of the Premier League. Some have even suggested Konsa and Gabriel have become the best partnership in world football, external.Arsenal already had seven senior defenders when they signed Konsa including one of the most solid and well-established partnerships in world football in Saliba and Gabriel.But in Saliba's absence, Konsa has started seven of Arsenal's nine Premier League matches, having joined just hours before their opening match against Coventry before coming on against former club Aston Villa for his debut. And Arteta has said the way that Konsa has settled for the Gunners has been "unbelievable". The defender made 286 appearances for Villa after joining in July 2019 from Brentford and helped them win the Europa League in May, the club's first European trophy since 1982.He has established himself as a first-choice starter for England and started seven of the eight games the Three Lions played at the World Cup. And what could now prove a big clue to his Arsenal future - he started the quarter-final against Norway at right back. Konsa is an imposing figure, quick across the ground, and his aggression in challenges has impressed supporters.The 29-year-old scored the opener against Everton in Arsenal's 2-0 win and put in another commanding performance as the Gunners beat Liverpool at Anfield for the first time in 14 years on Sunday.Arsenal host Hull on Saturday before the next international break starts this month. That time will allow Saliba to further build up his fitness before he will become a regular option again for Arteta. However, when Saliba does return, Arteta is going to have to disappoint someone.Ben White and Jurrien Timber have been Arsenal's first choice right-backs this season and are dependable top-level options. Both have previously had fitness issues but White has been available for all but one of Arsenal's games this campaign.Konsa could move to right-back, a position he also made his England debut in, which would allow Saliba to slot in next to Gabriel in his regular spot. Arteta values physicality in his Arsenal side and moving Konsa, who is physically imposing, to right-back would give opposition attackers a formidable challenge. Saliba's return also lowers the chance of game time for young centre-back Cristhian Mosquera and his low number of minutes so far this season will raise questions about his future, even though he has recovered from a hamstring injury. The Gunners played 63 games in all competitions last season as they won the league and reached the Champions League final. And, with Arteta aiming to defend the title and have European success this time out, there will be a lot of games for him to rotate his many options.

schema.headline: William Saliba's return gives Mikel Arteta selection headache at Arsenal

title: Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
description: The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for perma
body: The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost. Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save £10bn.But under revised plans described by the Tories as a "U-turn", some foreign care workers will continue to wait five years, and others will be able to seek a five-year extension.While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC they would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.In March, the Home Office said, external the net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at £10bn under existing rules.Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.She had previously argued that not delaying settlement for migrant care workers already in the UK would lead to a "£10bn drain on our public finances".Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least £25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.Just over 500,000 people will now be delayed from gaining permanent residency, down from almost 800,000 before Monday's changes. Some 1.9m people will settle in the UK between 2026 and 2030, according to the Home Office.Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship. Asked about the cost of her revised plans, the home secretary told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the detailed costs would be published when her department puts the changes before Parliament.In an interview recorded on Monday evening, she said the changes overall represented "savings in the billions" to the Department of Work and Pensions in people not claiming benefits."The reason for that is the cohort that was most likely to fall upon the state is that cohort of care workers not doing care work at the moment - if they'd settled at five years, many more of those would have gone on to claim benefits."That will now not happen because they will not be settling at five years - those individuals get a second chance to make that contribution that they originally came to make," she told Today.The Home Office's £10bn figure was based on an estimate by the Migration Advisory Committee of how much an average migrant care worker would cost the UK in benefits and public services throughout their lifetime.While Mahmood would not give a new savings figure, Home Office minister Anna Turley told BBC Breakfast it would be "at least £1bn over the next couple of years in terms of welfare savings" but "we'll be doing more calculations" on the total.The Conservatives said the "U-turn" would cost the UK billions of pounds.The £10bn figure has been criticised by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which found a £115bn addition, external to UK public finances under current settlement rules."Public debate has focused heavily on the costs of recent migration, but this is not the whole story," IPPR associate director Marley Morris said.Mahmood also declined to say whether Prime Minister Andy Burnham had told her to change tack on her proposals, which she had put forward in November under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.She told Today a public consultation had resulted in a "transformative package" that "strikes the right balance".She has denied Monday's move was a U-turn, and said the revised plans meant some 500,000 people already in the UK would now have to wait longer than five years to qualify for settlement.The exact wait will vary based on income and whether people arrived in the UK legally or illegally.Mahmood had faced criticism within the Labour Party for proposing to retrospectively change the rules for migrant workers already in the UK.Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had said it amounted to "chang[ing] the goalposts", while several MPs described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.

schema.headline: Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
